newsitem.title: INDIA: Militant says Kashmir hostages killed last year.
newsitem.headline: Militant says Kashmir hostages killed last year.

text.p: A captured guerrilla has told Indian authorities that four Westerners kidnapped in Kashmir two years ago were shot dead in early 1996 and buried in a cave, a pro-government militiaman and a newspaper said.

They said Nazir Ahmad Najar of the Harkat-ul-Ansar group told authorities of the murders after he was arrested last month in a joint operation involving police and a pro-government militia group called J.K. Ikhwan.

Najar, also known as Nazir Chhaan, said the four hostages were killed in Magam forest near Kokernag town, some 85 km (55 miles) south of the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir state, Srinagar, in January 1996, six months after they were captured.

"Nazir Chhaan told his interrogators all the four tourists were shot dead near Magam Kokernag and the only eyewitness to the scene is a government employee from Magam who has gone underground," Hilal Hayder, head of J.K. Ikhwan, told Reuters on Saturday in the town of Anantnag.
J.K. Ikhwan is one of several groups that help Indian security forces combat separatist militants in Jammu and Kashmir, mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.
Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan, American Donald Hutchings and German Dirk Hasert were abducted while trekking in the Himalayan region in July 1995 by a previously unknown group, Al-Faran.
Al-Faran beheaded a fifth hostage, Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe, in August 1995.
Negotiations between Indian authorities and the abductors broke off in late 1995, and officials and diplomats say they have no firm evidence to indicate whether the hostages are dead or alive.
Indian authorities and the hostages' relatives have said Al-Faran was backed by the Pakistan-based Harkat-ul-Ansar, which denies any links to Al-Faran.
A leading Kashmiri daily, the Daily Excelsior, carried a front-page article on Saturday on Najar's statements.
"Nazir, according to sources, said that on a chilly evening, the captors forced the entry of the four hostages into a blind cave and told them it was a tunnel," the newspaper said.

"As the hostages were leading into the cave, their captors fired pistol shots killing all the four on spot," it said, adding that Najar said the militants had sealed the entrance to the cave with mounds of clay.
Najar said there were six abductors, three of whom were still believed to be in the Magam area, present when the hostages were shot, and that a state government employee witnessed the killings.

Government officials and diplomats said they had been unable to confirm Najar's story, which resembled a statement made last year by another captured militant, Nazir Mohammad, who also said the hostages had been killed in Magam forest.

Indian and foreign experts used sniffer dogs from Germany last June to scour the forest but found no bodies. "The area last month was again thoroughly searched by our boys and police, but it was fruitless," Hayder said.
"We cross-check every report but so far we have not got any conclusive evidence whether the hostages are dead or alive," K.B. Jandial, the Jammu and Kashmir state government spokesman, said.
"We hope to come to some resolution to put this matter to rest, to know that they are alive or to find their bodies in order to put to rest the speculation," a Western diplomat said.
